In 1896, we admit that there was only spent by our predecessors $470,869 and that the expenditure increased in 1906 to $555,923, but, in 1896, they collected under $8,000,000 and in 1906 this government collected over $14,000,000 of revenue. Though there was an increase in expense to the country there was an enormous increase of revenue. Take the Department of Customs. In 1896, the then Minister of Cus-427
toms expended $896,000 and we have to admit that ten years later the expenditure was $1,548,000. But the revenue which was collected by the Department of Customs in 1896 was $19,000,000 while the revenue which my hon. friend the present Minister of Customs (Mr. Paterson) collected in 1906, was $46,000,000, so, my hon. friend ought in all fairness when he tells the people about this enormous increase in expenditure, to also tell them that in many of the departments these expenditures are met by corresponding increases in revenue. In regard to increases of expenditure generally, nobody expects that the Dominion of Canada is going to stand still. The increase in expenditures has had something to do-it has had much to do- with the increased development that has come upon this Dominion. If we had not built railways in various parts of the country could there have been that development? Could the Crow's Nest country have been developed if we had not put money into that



railway by large and liberal subsidies ? Could the western prairies have been filled up as they have been with immigrants from other lands if we had not spent money on immigration and the building up of our railways? Surely it must be evident that when we are spending these sums of money we are contributing to the development of the country. The needs of the country are large and varied. The west needs railways to open up the country, the lake and St. Lawrence districts need river and harbour improvements, and the maritime provinces require breakwaters and wharfs to facilitate trade and to protect the lives and property of the mariners and fishermen. At one point a public building is required to give reasonable accommodation to the public business; at another point an armoury is required in response to the military enthusiasm of the people. Those who wish to be sectional will see only their own need and not be willing to see the need of others. It will not do to make comparisons in that way. The duty of the government is to see the needs of the whole country. My hon. friend from North Toronto on one occasion made reference to our spending moneys at the little places in Canada. Sir, the mass of the people of Canada live in the little places. The needs of the cities are great and we are not unmindful of their interests, but whence come their progress and prosperity if not from the hamlets and villages scattered throughout the country and which originate the trade which passes through the great cities? The needs of the country are great and we are not forgetful of the great works or the little ones either. We are building the Transcontinental Railway and we are going to push on to completion this work which interests the whole country from ocean to ocean. We are going to build the Hudson Bay Railway and thus realize the expectations of the people of the west. We are" providing for the various needs of the country according to their respective requirements. It is the duty of a government, Sir, not to be sectional, not to think of this particular place or that, but to take a broad look throughout the whole country and adapt its policy to its needs. That is the policy which this government has followed. We look back to-night with pride and pleasure upon the twelve years of Liberal administration, upon the results of this policy we have adopted, and in the face of the splendid record, which any Liberal candidate can present to an audience in any part of Canada. I do not hesitate to say, Sir, that that policy will continue to command the support of an intelligent and patriotic people.

BORDEN (Carleton, Ont.) My hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) has made us a stump speech and he has opened it up by telling us a little story about the wolf at the door. Well, I Mr. FIELDING.
may say to my hon. friend that I do not think he can be called a watch dog as far as the public treasury is concerned nor can lie be compared with the man who once guarded the public treasury, Alexander Mackenzie, and whose record and experience in days gone by have been made public in this country by a letter which was published shortly after 1875. My hon. friend refers to historic incidents and fables. I would think he might have referred to the days of old when a king and his courtiers banqueted and feasted while the enemy was at the gate and the handwriting was on the wall. The Minister of Finance pumped up his courage tonight, because, notwithstanding all his boasting, notwithstanding all the vain glorious promises as to what his government will accomplish in the future, and all the vain glorious references to what he has accomplished in the past, he knows that the trend of public opinion in Canada to-day is against him. He has referred to the financial situation of the country. He failed to tell us however, how he expects to meet the $200,000,000 to $250,000,000 of obligations which must be met by this country within the next two or three years. Before I sit down I will read to him some words from the London ' Economist ' which go as far in their condemnation of the record of this government as any words uttered by my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster). He boasts of his loans. He is proud, Mr. Speaker, that a loan of this Dominion of Canada placed on the London market was taken up only to the extent of forty-four per cent. He actually boasts here to-night of the fact that withiu the past year the government has been paying six per cent at the Bank of England and apparently he does not understand how much that reflects on his lack of foresight in not preparing for the financial stringency which was foreseen by every important business interest in the country, but was not foreseen by the Minister of Finance for Canada. He boasts of the fact that he placed a loan on the London market that lie had to go to financial underwriters in London and that only forty-four per cent of it was taken up.
He boasts of. the position of Canadian securities to-day under his management, but let us look at another comparis-son. A Canadian loan, backed by all the enormous resources of this country but handicapped with the evil financial record of this government, was subscribed for to the extent of only 44 per cent or less than one-half. At about the same time the Irish land loan was placed on the London market by the British government and it was subscribed for between seventy and eighty times over. My authority is the LondLon ' Morning Post,' of July 8. 1908. Is the Minister of Finance proud of that ? What has he to say with regard to it ? Nothing. What has he to say with respect to the conditions when the new loans fall

due within the next few years ? The Minister of Finance says nothing, but the London ' Economist ' has something to say and I shall quote from that journal a few words which may serve to tone down the enthusiasm of gentlemen opposite, and which may also serve to enlighten the people of this country as to the opinion which will be held by the great financiers of London of the future financial standing of Canada should the present rate of expenditure be maintained. After referring to the great progress Canada has made in recent years ; after referring incidentally to the fact that the public debt of Canada is now four times greater per head than that of the United States, the article continues :
The country in short has been making rapid progress and is well able to carry its burdens provided there is no monstrous addition in Hie immediate future.
The article goes on to enumerate the great public works and undertakings which this government proposes, and it continues:
Here-deducting what has already been spent by the government on account of its section of the Grand Trunk Pacific-is a total of not far from two hundred million dollars to be raised in London before long, to say nothing of the considerable aggregate of Dominion debts falling due, or of the possible necessity for borrowing for other services now that the era of buoyant revenues is over.
I invite the special attention of the Minister of Finance, and the special attention of the Prime Minister, and above all the special attention of the members of this parliament and the people of the country to tlie words which follow :
This, it must be allowed, is a staggering outlook. Instead of economizing the govern. ment has gone on increasing debt and expenditure as a means of mitigating depression ; always a risky policy.
And in the face of that opinion from an impartial and well informed. source-because the London ' Economist ' is recognized as one of the greatest financial authorities in the world-the Minister of Finance en-tei'taius this House with a stump speech, and he gives not one word of information as to how these enormous obligations will be discharged. I was amazed that a gentleman occupying his position should not in the course of an hours' speech give one word of information to the people of Canada as to how these enormous burdens are to be met in the future. Not a word of comment on them, not a word of explanation, not a word as to provision for the future, but many words in idle taunts against some half dozen members on this side of the House who had asked for legitimate expenditure of public monevs in their constituencies. Sir. we on this side of the House have not objected and do not object 4274
to proper and legitimate expenditures, but we do object to the expenditures of this government in countless instances for the past ten or twelve years for purposes which are not in the public interest and which the Minister of Finance knew were not in the public interest when he sanctioned and authorized them. I was told of one instance, out of hundreds in his own constituency, where an opponent of the Minister of Finance at an election in his county went to a certain voter and inquired as to how he intended to vote and this gentleman who had previously supported the Minister of Finance was not well satisfied. Why, he said, Mr. Fielding means well; he has built this breakwater as a means of giving more employment but he knew and we all knew that it was of no possible use, and why did not Mr. Fielding take that money and divide it amongst us. I say we do not object to legitimate expenditure but we do object to middlemen's profits. The Minister of Finance has declared that there is a new Canada to-day, a new Canada which was not born until after 1896. Weil, Mr. Speaker, there is a new Canada and there is a new sign at the door of almost every department in the public service, and it*is a sign to the middleman : Apply here. That invitation to the middleman has not been neglected by that very numerous class, and they have been well rewarded.
The hon. gentleman referred to a great many subjects in the course of his speech, but he omitted to refer to a great many more. To a certain extent he dealt with one or two important subjects, but he dealt with tlthm in a small way. He spoke of the enormous expenditure by the government of Canada in recent years, hut he did not mention the fact that the government has taken out of the pockets of the people during the past twelve years $252,000,000 more than the taxation would have amounted to upon the basis that existed in 1896. And where has this money gone ? Look around this country and point me to any great enterprise that has been completed and paid for. I admit that something has been done by the government in improving the canals, in continuation of a policy initiated by their Conservative predecessors. I admit that the Intercolonial has been extended to Montreal, that some public buildings have been erected through the country, and that something has been done for the St. Lawrence route. I do not desire to minimize in the least anything the government has done in the way of legitimate expenditure for public works, but look at the great public works that are now proposed by the government and which have not been paid for, or paid for in only small part. Look at the Transcontinental Railway : it will cost nearly $200,000,000 of which we have paid up to the present time only $26,000,000. Look at the Geor-

gian bay canal, which these hon. gentlemen flaunt before the country whenever they think it expedient to do so ; look at the Welland canal which they are proposing to build, in their speeches out of parliament if not in parliament ; look at the necessary but unaccomplished development of our ports ; look at the proposal for building the Hudson Bay Railway; look at dozens of other great and important and necessary public works in this country, the expenditures on which the country will have to face during the next few years, and ask yourselves whether or not, having regard to the enormous increase of taxatiou within the past twelve years, the country has received any fair and adequate return for that money which has come out of the pockets of its taxpayers.
My hon. friend dealt among other things with the Transcontinental Railway. He did not dwell upon it to any very great extent ; but I desire to say one or two words with regard to it, for the purpose of placing before the people of this country the ideas of the Finance Minister and the principles upon which the government propose to deal with capital expenditure. In a recent debate in this House my hon. friend was good enough to refer to some statements made by me as the cost of that road as ' monstrous representations ' or some similar phrase, and I think it is well to look a little at the cost of that road and at the views of the Minister of Finance with regard to it. What is the position which we take with regard to the cost of that road ? We point out in the first place that whereas the Minister of Finance estimated the cost of the road from Winnipeg to Moncton at $51,300,000, it is now admitted by the Minister of Railways and the Minister of Finance that without taking into consideration interest, or terminals, or anything execept the bare cost of the road it will amount to $114,500,000. X take that as the cost of the road to the country, because some one must pay for that road, and there is no one to pay for it, so far as I am aware, except the people of this country. The Minister of Finance says that that is a complete mistake and a monstrous statement to place before the people of this country. In order not to do him injustice, I will use his own words :
Let me say at once that it is a monstrous statement to say that that represents the cost of that road to Canada.
And he concludes his sentence by saying:
Therefore you must strike it out entirely.
of Finance estimated, or $114,500,000, as the reality proves. Further than that, if you are to strike out that item entirely, as the Minister of Finance argues, then it would not make the slightest difference to the people of this country whether the road cost $250,000,000, and therefore all inquiry into Major Hodgins' charges or into the Grand Trunk Pa.cific complaints is utterly idle. Would any one imagine that these were sober words proceeding from the mouth of the Minister of Finance of Canada. One would imagine that language of that kind could only come from some person who was entirely reckless or regardless of his words and absolutely void of any responsibility for the effect they produce. But mv hon. friend went further. He said that interest on construction should be struck out for the same reason. Therefore it necessarily follows that it makes not the slightest difference to the people of this country whether they pay 10 per cent or 3 per cent on the cost of construction. Does the Minister of Finance or anyone else imagine that the people- of this country can be deceived by an argument of that kind ? I concur in the view that has been taken by many gentlemen on this side of the House that in placing the cost of the National Transcontinental Railway at about $192,000,000, I have placed it very much below the mark ; that when the people of this country come to foot the bill, it will be found that the amount which I named, and which as the hon. member for North Toronto truly says is only an estimate, will be found very much below the mark.
Mr. Speaker, it is rather a grave situation that confronts the people of Canada to-day. My hon. friend boasts of bis revenues. Let me read one or two further paragraphs from the article in the London ' Economist ' to which I alluded a moment ao-o.	After dealing with the attemptswhich have been made to settle the great northern portions of this country the article uses this language :
The tendency is to push railways further and further north into the solitudes lying above the main line of the Grand Trunk Pacific in Ontario, Quebec and British Columbia, where development even under the most favourable circumstances, is bound to be slow; and schemes are actually on foot for invading Labrador and TJngara. The higher price we h-ave to pay for money in England may deter the federal and provincial governments from voting cash subsidies to such projects, but some of them are certain to obtain guarantees, which may easily prove embarrassing.
' Let us look at that for a moment. In considering the cost of the Transcontinental Railway you must strike out that item entirely ; what follows ? This follows : That it makes not the slightest difference to this country whether that road costs $51,300,000 as the Minister Mr. R. L BORDEN.
My hou. friend the Minister of Finance puts to one side with a wave of his hand the liabilities which this country has assumed aud which it is proposing to assume in respect to these guarantees of great undertakings. That is not the view that is taken by- the article I have quoted

from this great financial journal, which declares that these guarantees may well prove embarrassing. The Minister of Finance has a different outlook and a different view entirely to that entertained with regard to these conditions by this great financial journal. Further on in the same article it says :
Hereafter we are likely to get into trouble over the government end of the Grand Trunk Pacific. Many in parliament are of opinion that the company, which has agreed to pay an annual rental equal to 3 per cent on cost for this portion, will be obliged to back out of its bargain. It does not begin paying rent till some time after the completion of the road, but recent explorations have not revealed any great timber or mineral wealth along the route between Winnipeg and Quebec, whilst the division from Quebec to Moncton can hardly be remunerative in view of the competition of the Intercolonial, a government line barely meeting operating expenses. On all sides it is felt that the government should have been content with the company's original design, to begin at North Bay and go on bo the Pacific. North Bay being a terminal of the Grand Trunk proper. Unfortunately, the government yielded to party and sectional pressure.
And this Is comment from a great financial journal upon the action of that gentleman who to-night boasted that this government was never under any conditions subject to sectional prejudices. The article continues as follows :
The company intended, of course, to live honourably up to its covenant, but circumstances may force it sooner or later to ask to be relieved of the stretch of 1,000 miles from Moncton to North Bay-such, at least, is the growing impression, in which event Canada will be saddled with another white elephant. This, however, is a matter for the future. I mention it merely to strengthen the argument that we had better go slow, and let the remote north remain unopened till we have fulfilled the obligatons, direct or incidental, undertaken in behalf of other parts of the Dominion.

Mr. Farrer salaried by the Canadian Pacific Railway.

The hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) has placed an exhaustive statement of the position before the House. So far as the important and significant portions of that statement are concerned, the Finance Minister, has made no attempt to meet them. They relate Mr. R. L. BORDEN
in the first place to the rapidly increasing expenditures of this country; in the second place to the tendency of this administration to increase that expenditure still further in the face of falling revenues ; and in the third place to the necessity of meeting loans in the London market of bet ween two and three hundred millions during the next three or four or five years. These all-iro-portant points have not been grappled with by the Finance Minister who has uttered no word with regard to them, yet in the significant and pregnant words of the article I read here to-night it is these matters which are engaging the attention of financiers in the great money markets of the world although they are not engaging the attention of the government of this country. These are considerations which it was proper to place before the House at the close of the session and when we come to realize what the proposed expenditures of the government amount to I say that no hon. gentleman who reads the resolution and takes to heart the enormous figures of expenditure and the necessary increase of the public debt in the resolution, can find it consistent with his duty to vote against the resolution proposed.

One word in reply to a statement made by the Minister of Finance referring to myself. I am satisfied that the minister would not willingly misrepresent me and must have made his statement from hearsay, relying on the report of some person who was present in the House when the discussion took place. Had he taken the trouble to read * Hansard ' he would not have made the statement that he did and I presume when he made that statement reflecting on myself the same application might be made to the hon. gentlemen on this side to whom he referred. I shall read for his information what took place. We were discussing the militia estimates. And I made this statement :

It is fair to assume that these armouries will cost about $10,000 apiece and this vote of $50,000 will therefore erect five armouries.	.
The Minister of Militia had a vote in the estimates of $50,000 for armouries. I made this reference to it :
I would like to know where the minister is going to place these. I want to remind him that they ought to put Gananoque in as good a position as the government found it in when they came into power. We have at Gananoque a battery and a company of rifles. When this government came into power we had a first-class'drill shed and armoury, but the government saw fit to tear it down and to pu'roh'ase another site.
And they promised to build another armoury in its place. That was eleven years ago, and they have done nothing. I asked that $10,000 of this $50,000 that was being devoted to the construction of arinoui/les

might be used to carry out the promise of the government to replace the armoury in Gananoque which they had torn down. But the promise they made, like every other promise which they have made, has been left unfulfilled. They took the whole $50,000 for buildings in constituencies of their supporters and neglected the pledge that they had made to Gananoque. The bon. minister says that I made application for an expenditure of public money. All I asked was they should keep the promise they made. In the course of the debate there was the following :
What about carrying out your arrangement at Gananoque?
I will put that on the list when I return to my office in the morning.

Gananoque should be the first on the list because we had a drill shed iand armoury there and the minister tore it down. He bought a site but he has not given the boys an armoury since.
The minister says that this is an application for public expenditure. I asked this government to carry out the promise and replace the armoury that they had torn down, and the minister acknowledged the corn.

I wish to put on record my disapproval of what I am bound to call the unwarranted and extraordinary expenditure of public money by the government now in power. My name has been mentioned here to-night as asking for a wharf at Brighton village. I am justified in asking for it. I did not ask for a wharf where there is no'water. I did not ask for a wharf in an inland lake. I did not ask for a wharf which would turn into a bridge in the course of construction. I did not ask for a wharf to cost $13,000 at a little village on Lake Huron where the postal revenue is $10.14 per annum. I asked for a wharf where it is really needed in the interest of the public, and I say it is a shame and a disgrace to the government in power that they have not built a wharf at Brighton. It is a village of 1,800 inhabitants, with a large trade. I pointed out the need publicly in this House. I did not wait on the minister privately, but I went with a deputation who laid the matter before him. And he gave the deputation to understand that something would be done. I fully expected that there would be an item in the supplementary estimates for a wharf at Brighton village. I am surprised that it was not brought down, because the Minister of Public Works stated in the House that his policy was to spend money where it is needed. I cannot believe that that is his policy, because he has not carried that out in the case of Brighton village.
One can hardly realize that the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) were at that great Reform convention held here in Ottawa in 1893. They were greatly alarmed at that time at what they called the large expenditure-which happened to be about $42,000,000. And, if I remember rightly the speeches of the Prime Minister in the campaign of 1896 in the province of Ontario, he told the people he was greatly alarmed at the annual expenditure and promised that if his party were given the reins of power, lie would reduce the annual expenditure $2,000,000 or $3,000,000. I believe the people are surprised at what the right hon. Prime Minister is doing. If he was alarmed in 1896, they are alarmed now. I am safe in saying that no parliamentarian, however long he may have sat in this House, lias ever seen that wilfully wasteful expenditure of public money as we have witnessed this session. I am not one of those who do not believe in the development of the country. I believe in spending money for the development, but I do not believe in wasteful expenditure. It has been proven in this House time and again that money has been expended, not in the best interests of the people of this country, but mostly in the interest of the middlemen. As stated by an hon. member this evening, we have middlemen rapping at the door of every department, and every one of them has had his wishes gratified. That is not expending money in the public interest ; and I protest against such wasteful and extravagant expenditure.

The Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) speaking with regard to the correspondent of the 'Economist,' led the House to believe that there is a great difference between the casual correspondent and the editor of a responsible journal. But this was not written by a casual correspondent. I have it before me and it is headed ' From our Correspondent.4 It is nof signed but is adopted by the paper as expressing the views of the paper. It carries with it all the weight of an editorial in that journal.

The question which my hon. friend has alluded to is one which is of very great importance to Canada and he will agree with me when I tell him that I have always taken a deep interest in the Soo industry. Before I came to this House and while acting in another sphere I went to a considerable length in doing what I could to see that that important industry was retained and maintained for the people of Canada. Although at the present moment the conditions are not just what I would like I still have faith in the Soo industry and we want to provide the largest possible share of orders for its product. We have two of these industries in Canada, one at Sydney and the other at the Soo. I am sure if my hon. friend will consult those interested in the Soo industry they will tell him that this government has shown its friendship to their industry in a very practical way. On two occasions at least since I have had charge of the Railway Department we have endeavoured to make it smoother for the Soo industry than it might have been if we had not made that endeavour. I believe with him that the steel rails made at Sydney and at Sault Ste. Marie are equal to any made on the continent. I am perfectly in sympathy with that view. I do not agree with the article read by my hon. friend which says that steel rails made in the United States are inferior because they make some magnificent rails there. I will communicate with the president or general manager of the Grand Trunk Pacific to see if there is any truth in the report that orders for rails have been given to the United States makers. I am
Possibly the minister is familiar with the firms who are importing, but there is no getting away from the fact that there are and have been a lot of very heavy importations of steel rails from the United States, some of which at least have been specially imported for use upon the western division of the Grand Trunk Pacific. In contrast with that let nie remind the minister of a statement made by Sir Thomas Shaughnes-sy, president of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, in the famous speech that he made in Toronto not long ago at the celebration of the opening of the Toronto Sudbury line in which he said that every rail, s spike, bridge, tie, car and locomotive was of Canadian production and that despatch and quality of the Canadian product were equal to the very best. Marie, in Nova Scotia, and at Port Arthur and in connection with many other steel and iron industries, in which a large amount of Canadian, British and American capital is invested. I would ask him to give these matters his very serious consideration and do what he can now, to show the Canadian spirit which should and perhaps will influence him in the matter. to see that the terms of the agreement between this company and the government are strictly adhered to in spirit as well as in letter, that our Canadian industries get the full benefit of the work of the construction of that great road and that all materials and supplies which are the product of Canadian industries are used in the construction of the road, provided the condi-

anxious to do wliat X can to see that the rails to be used on Canada's great Transcontinental Railway shall be produced in the Dominion of Canada.

This is the last opportunity I shall have to ask the Minister of Railways and Canals a question that I asked once or twice before as to whether he has been able to find the report of the engineer who was sent out last fall to inspect the Canadian Northern Railway between Irwood and the Pas Mission '!
Yesterday I placed on the desk of my hon. friend the report of our engineer dated February last and that Is the only report we have in the department.
Last autumn I met a gentleman on the Canadian Northern and he told me he had been commissioned by the government to go over that road, and he gave a very graphic description of his trip.
Perhaps it refers to the same report ; was it Mr. McArthur ?

No, it was Mr. Paradis. He gave me a graphic description of his trip as he would to an old friend, for I have known him for many years and he told me the land was swamp, and that nothing could be hauled over the line in the summer season until the whole country was drained. He told me a hand-car was the heaviest thing they could run over a considerable part of the line and that they had laid the rails so that when the frost came they could take a train of materials out. The report which the minister refers to was made by a gentleman who was sent out there after the freeze up and when there was a foot of snow on the ground. I should like to know if it is possible that a subsidy of 12.800 acres per mile, and which the Minister of the Interior says' has been selected in western Saskatchewan, could have been given to such a railroad as that.

As this is the last occasion we will have to question the government, I would like the Minister of Railways to give me the information he promised with regard to the present condition of the Robert syndicate lease.
I had a copy of the lease in the House last night.

The lease has been in my possession since it was signed, but I want to know what has been done under it. Has the Robert syndicate made its payment to the government, and are they Mr. GRAHAM.
carrying out the conditions of the lease. A company called the Canadian Light and Power Company is applying to the city council of Montreal to light the city, and that company is supposed to be the Robert syndicate under another name. As I understand it the Robert syndicate cannot under the terms of the lease amalgamate with the Montreal Light, Heat and Power Company according to clause 16 of the lease. Their lease is very stringent on that point, and I would like to know if the Minister of Railways has been notified of any change ?
I will have to ask information from my hon. friend (Mr. Bergeron) what does the lease say about that ?

In order to protect the people of Montreal against monopoly the clause 16 of the lease says : The Robert syndicate shall not amalgamate with the Montreal Light, Heat and Power Company, and it is commonly supposed in Montreal that the Canadian Light and Power Company which is negotiating with the city council is in reality the Robert syndicate. I do not believe they could do that without the authorization of the Minister of Railways.

I imagine not. If the lease says they shall not amalgamate with a certain company that would seem to imply that they could with some other company, but anyway I think it would not be done without notifying the department and I have had no such Information.

The Robert syndicate cannot amalgamate with the Montreal Light, Heat and Power Company, but the Canadian Light and Power Company might. A subterfuge of that kind would be tantamount to bad faith on the part of the syndicate and I should think the Minister of Railways would know something about it.
We have no information in the department with regard to that but I shall make inquries. They have paid $6,000 and another $6,000 is due on the 1st of July and I presume will be paid in due course.

The Minister of Railways said some days ago that he would tell me before the close of the session what he would do in reference to building a short stretch of canal near the village of Bradford in south Simcoe. I would be glad if I could tell the people interested that the Minister of Railways had decided to construct that small piece of work.

I do not think I promised my hon. friend that I would tell him what

I would do ; but I did look into tlie matter and I find that the report shows the mileage to be greater than my hon. friend had supposed.
Three-quarters of a mile?
It is about three times that. I had an approximate estimate made but it is not one on which we can rely. We will have to consider the matter as we proceed with the work of the canal.

After the close of the session the minister will have very little to do, and if I write to him would he answer me and let me know what he intends ? When we spoke of it some days ago the chief engineer was ill and the minister could not give any information about the matter.

I know my hon. friend (Mr. Lennox) will write me a very courteous letter and if he does I will give him all the information I possibly can in reply. I would not like to commit myself to anything because I really do not know what I am in a position to say.

Resolution reported.
Bill (No. 215) to authorize the granting of subsidies in aid of the construction of lines of railway therein mentioned-Mr. Graham -read the second time, and House went into committee thereon.
Is the Bill in the same form as the resolutions?
Yes.
I asked if any of the roads proposed to be subsidized are now actually under construction.

I endeavoured to get all the information I could along that line. I find the following are partly constructed or under construction, Nos. 32,40,43 (three miles), 45, (a portion constructed, balance under construction), 55 (two miles under construction), 60 (a portion under construction). 61, (a portion under construction), 62, 65 (four miles), 66 and 68 (under construction). An hon. gentleman asked the mileage of each of the great railways under this. I cannot guarantee the accuracy of these figures as tlie subsidies are sometimes voted under names of other companies, but my clerk figures it in this way:
Miles.
Grand Trunk Pacific	 330-9
Canadian Northern Railway	 202-9
Canadian Pacific Railway	 270-15

I could not get access to these applications this morning and consequently cannot say much as to their contents. Taking a view of the items which I have had some opportunity of examining I observe that No. 39 provides for a subsidy

to the Canadian Pacific Railway in respect of 34J miles. Section 40 provides for a subsidy for the Canadian Pacific Railway for 123 miles. So far as the Canadian Pacific Railway is concerned. I have never known it to have difficulty in carrying out its undertakings in respect to the building of branch lines. It is a very wealthy and prosperous company. Its stock is considerably above par, standing at 150 or 160; it pays 7 per cent and so far as my memory goes' its officers have publicly announced that in the larger portions of Canada to-day railway building should be carried on without assistance from the government. I observe further in respect of 123 miles to be built by the Canadian Pacific Railway, that the information contained in the documents on the table is very meagre. It states that the road is already under construction; if that is so I would be of opinion that that railway is quite able to carry the construction of that road to a conclusion. I do not observe from the documents before the House that there is any application by the Canadian Pacific Railway. It does not purport to be signed by any person. No. 68 relates to sixty miles of the Canadian Northern from Hawkesbury to Ottawa which, I understand, is partially completed. The same thing is true of items 49 and 62 which are to aid branch lines of the Grand Trunk Pacific. Item 62, is for a branch line from Port Arthur to the main line of the Transcontinental Railway. That is distinctly a part of the enterprise of the Grand Trunk Pacific, as will appear by reference to the statute under which the Grand Trunk Pacific was incorporated, section 12 of chapter 122 of the Acts of 1903. I refer to section 12 of that Act. which I would read if it were not that I desire to economze the time of the House. The same observation will apply to No. 49 which is distinctly a part of the Grand Trunk Pacific. I have not been able to look at the application with regard to that particular item. But an hon. member who looked into it informed me that there is no application excepting a very informal one purporting to be made by the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) I do not vouch for that of mv own information, for I could not find the document.
That is all the information it gives.

Here, for instance, is the way the application reads in part :
Name of railway. A railway.
Province. The province of Quebec.
What subsidy applied for? 200 miles.
8.	Prom Montreal to a point on the Transcontinental.
9.	Applicant. Sir Wilfrid Laurier.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. R. L. Borden) will remember that I explained that it was put in this way only to show that there was an application.

This subsidy was granted in response to one of the largest deputations that have visited us this session, and who urged it very strongly. That is the reason it was informal-it was put that way merely to keep the record.
I am only dealing with the information that lias been laid on the table.
I explained that fully last night.

I was not aware of It. It must have been at the time when I was absent from the chamber. The points I take with regard to these five items- which are the only ones I have had an opportunity to look into-is that they must necessarily be built by the railway companies to whom subsidies are proposed to be paid. So far as that point is concerned. I might be permitted to allude to some observations made in this House by the exMinister of Railways and Canals, my hon. friend from Westmoreland (Mr. Eimmer-son). I quote from ' Hansard ' of 1906. page 5965 :
I recognize that the Grand Trunk Pacific came in 1903 o>r 1904 and asked authority from this parliament to build certain branch lines as weU as to have the lease from the government of Canada. They asked authority from the government of Canada, when it should have constructed a trunk line from Winnipeg to Moncton, to lease and operate that trunk line. A part of the scheme and arrangement and agreement on the part of the Grand Trunk Pacific was that they should build certain branch lines; and they are held to that agreement.
And further on ;
The Grand Trunk Pacific Company are bound to build it; they are under obligation.
This is with reference to a line to the city of St. John. He deals with that exactly as with the other line. He is referring to the two branch lines to which I have alluded, and an additional one to the city of St. John. And he says that the Grand Trunk Pacific are ' under obligation.' The report proceeds :
Under what charter?

Under every discussion that was held in this House in 1903 and 1904. They are under a moral obligation, more than that they are under a pledge, by reason of the project in its entirety. They asked for authority to build certain branch lines.
Will the hon. gentleman be kind enough to tell me where we shall find the statute that contains that?

I am not putting that claim forward. It was not within the statute, but it wa.s within the agreement, and a well understood agreement, and they are bound to do it.

That was the view of the government, as expressed by the then Minister of Railways, as regards the two lines, for both are included, I take it. I am not taking the point that railway subsidies should not be granted where absolutely necessary for the purpose of proper and legitimate railway development in this country. But I do take the point that where wealthy railway corporations need branch lines which would be carried to completion without a subsidy from the government, or where the company is under the business necessity o'f building these lines as part of its system, or under some arrangement or agreement with the government, it seems to me that we are going rather far in subsidizing such lines and making a heavy drain upon the revenues of the country. Looking at the live items I have mentioned, two are subsidies for the Canadian Pacific Railway, one for the Canadian Northern Railway and two others for the Grand Trunk Pacific. I find that the total amount of these subsidies authorized by the resolution and Bill is a little over $4,000,000, which is a pretty large sum and a pretty serious obligation. It might turn out, of course, that the roads will cost less than $22,000 a mile, in which case the amount of subsidy would be less, but the total subsidy authorized is no less than $4,079,000. I do not know how many more instances of- this kind would develop [DOT] if one had a proper opportunity .to investigate every one of these applications. I deeply regret that, within the time allowed, it is impossible to make such an investigation, and that the information brought down is of so scanty and unsatisfactory a character. My hon. friend the Minister of Railways and 'Canals may be able to give some information with respect of the five lines of which I speak. In the absence of information it does not seem to me that the government has any justification for proposing to subsidize lines which, so far as the facts before the House indicate, would be built in any case without aid from the government.

With reference to the two Canadian Pacific Railway lines, one has slipped my memory at the moment, and the one is of 123 miles in length and will not run over $3,200 a mile, as it Is in prairie country north of Moosejaw. But, as the committee will remember, earlier in the session, a very strong plea was made to the Railway Department to urge the Canadian Pacific Railway to build a line 123 miles of north of Moosejaw. The reason was that the company had gone so far as to let the contract a year or two ago and people had rushed in there in great numbers. But for some reason it was cancelled. Apparently the road was not going to be built. I took up the question with the Canadian Pacific Railway authorities, and they announced
that they would proceed with the building of the ix)ad. That was accompanied by a request that if the government were giving subsidies to that kind of a road, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company should be treated as other roads were treated. I thought so myself, and I put it in the list. The other one was applied for by the Canadian Pacific Railway themselves directly.
I made what inquiry I could, and I was assured that it was a road that would serve the people and ought to he aided. Now there is this question as to granting subsidies to a road -partly constructed, or that would be. Looking at it from one point of view, my hon. friend would he right, hut that has not been the view held bv the various governments. I find case after case where subsidies have been given to roads already constructed and in operation. If a country needs opening up by a railway, and a railway company is ready to go on with that, knowing that the policy of the government of Canada has been so far to aid railways, and if they proceeded on that assumption, I am inclined to think that it would not be a wise policy to say that because they went on with the work we should not aid i't, if it is doing similar work to other roads that are aided. The road from Montreal is not a Grand Trunk Pacific road, it is not so in stated terms. I suppose their charter giving them the right to build braoh lines would possibly be the only one at the present time. But in answer to a deputation, all that we said was that we would consider the advisability of aiding a line connecting the Transcontinental with Montreal. I was careful to put it in that way. It is necessary, both for the citv of Montreal and for that portion of Canada, as well as for the success of the road, that the connection should be made. Of the Canadian Northern between Montreal and Hawkesbury and Hawkesbury and Ottawa, quite a portion is graded, and the remarks I made a moment ago would apply to that. Work on * that road ceased some little time agio. However, I feel this way, possibly I may be wrong, but believing that we must before many years, notwithstanding all that has been said, have another line across the continent on Canadian territory, this being a portion of it, as it will be when it is linked up, and having aided the other two lines, I think it is only fair that we should aid this one. A part of the grading has been done. Taking, however, the view I expressed a few moments ago, that even if some work has been done on a road, it should not be a bar to getting assistance, if doing the same work. I was in favour of granting a subsidy to that line.

When there was under consideration the other evening a proposition to build a branch line on Prince

Edward Island connecting with the main Prince Edward Island Railway, I submitted as a proposition for the consideration of the government that they should first determine with respect to branch lines already constructed and connected with their government system. The Minister of Railways and Canals on that occasion said he had very strong personal views with respect to branch lines. I need not quote what he stated, but it will be within the memory of hon. gentlemen that he personally spoke favourably with respect to them, and he said that another announcement would be made in connection writh that subject. Yesterday I had occasion to make some remarks when the resolutions upon which this Bill is founded were under consideration. I then asked the government as to their ideas with respect to the branch lines themselves, because while I take no objection to the policy of aiding railways so far as this country can do so, and while I am in favour of that policy, yet it seems to me there should be certain limitations. Furthermore, I think that in determining as to the advanced ground that should be taken by this parliament in relation to aiding additional lines, there should first be considered the position and the condition of the branch lines already constructed, and which have been aided financially by this government. Now the Minister of Railways has stated that he is favourable to aiding the construction of the line of railway between Montreal and the city of Ottawa. His reasons therefor were that this portion between Montreal and Ottawa would undoubtedly be a part of a third transcontinental line of railway. He is aware that there are to-day already running between this city and Montreal three lines of railway, two of them it is true owned by one company and the other owned by the Grand Trunk Railway Company, formerly known as the Canada Atlantic Railway. Now it would seem to me that it is a matter of very serious consideration whether the government, in taking this forward movement, should not first deal with the branch lines, and with its own railway system. The Minister of Railways is disposed to aid a trunk line, the Canadian Northern, and very properly. I take no exception to that. But it seems to me that the government for whom he speaks should take into consideration the Intercolonial, and the relationship which exists between that railway and the lines now connected with it. Now, my hon. friend the Minister of Railways promised a later declaration with respect to the matter, and we had from the right hon. gentleman leading the House, yesterday, in answer to a question put by me, a statement as to the course that the government would take in the matter. The government accepted the principle as one that would be in the interests of the country and as one that would be adopted. The proposition would be Mr. EMMERSON.
adopted if the Intercolonial Railway were owned by a private corporation and that is a business proposition which must be acceptable to the country and in the interests of the country. He stated that
The matter has been given a good deal of consideration, but we have not yet been able to make np our minds that it is a policy we should adopt. Whilst we are not prepared to say bo my hon. friend

That is referring to myself-
-that we shall adopt this policy, we realize that it is one which requires consideration and makes it inouimibent upon the government to make the fullest inquiry in order that we may be in a position to discuss the matter adequately at another session.
That declaration may mean a good deal. There is a statement that an inquiry will be had, and I think it is due to this committee, as it is due to the country, that the nature of that inquiry should be disclosed. The government apparently have given the matter a good deal of consideration and they realize that it is a policy that requires consideration and places upon the government the responsibility of making the fullest inquiry in order that the matter may he considered at the next session or at another session. We are asked to deal with these propositions. There are railways that may be aided. Certainly we are incurring obligations with respect to certain proposed railways. We should not lose sight of the railways which we have already constructed, the railways in the eastern section of Canada and the railways that were constructed as feeders of the Intercolonial Railway and which were very largely constructed because of the fact that they would be feeders. I had occasion at the last session of this parliament to invite the attention of the House to the statements made by Sir Charles Tapper when he was asking assistance for the construction of certain of these lines and he justified that aid and assistance, properly so, by the fact that these lines would be feeders. I do not propose to take up the time of the committee by going fully into the question, but I think it might fairly be accepted on all sides that the Intercoio nial Railway has not been rounded out and will never be rounded out until it has control of its sphere of influence, until it has the control and management of the lines which may serve and which do measurably serve as feeders. In the interest of that section of the country these lines should be operated by the Intercolonial Railway. Now, I would like to ask the minister if he can acquaint this committee with the character of the investigation which is to he made. I quite appreciate the fact that no government should acquire any railways as feeders, that no government should acquire any of these branch lines without first getting tlie fullest possible information, without

first knowing what they were doing and then that they could only acquire them as a business proposition. I simply put that question to the minister, and I trust that he will take us and the country into his confidence with respect to the proposed inquiry. I ask if the government intend to have that inquiry and if they intend to have it at once ?

The question of branch railways, I have discovered, during the short time that I have been in this department, is one that is very vital particularly along the line of the Intercolonial Railway. If the Intercolonial Railway were run by a company there are branch lines now that would be a part of that system. The government railway is under somewhat different conditions possibly, but if the Intercolonial Railway is to retain its position it is worth while to very seriously consider if it ought not to go that far in carrying out business principles in order to see that it gets the traffic that rightly belongs to it. If, in the maritime provinces, keen competition should arise with the Intercolonial Railway we might wake up some morning possibly and find that another line had the branch lines and consequently the business that they now give to the Intercolonial Railway in a minor way. This is a large question. It affects Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Quebec. In all there are in the railways that would be called branches about 1,200 miles. There has been a report upon the branch lines of New Brunswick made at the request of the government of New Brunswick. That report I have. In short this is what I propose to do : In order to get the information that would be a basis to work on, it will be necessary to ascertain the length of each line, the amount of its traffic, its revenue, expenditure, rolling stock, the condition of the road and the probability of the development of business along the line.
What option there is on the line.
The option possibly. .
And who holds the option ?

These things would have to be investigated thoroughly, and I assume that the investigation would be along the line of getting this information so that we would be in a position to discuss iin a business way the question as to whether we should take over these branch lines. During the recess I propose to have such an investigation made.

The Minister of Railways and Canals has proved himself a most excellent jollier. The minister says that he has already in his hands a report from the commission appointed by the late government in tiie province of New Brunswick in
regard to branch lines. I have no doubt that report was a very full and exhaustive one because the gentleman who acted on that commission received a very handsome honorarium and I know he is a man of ability and I believe he made a thorough examination.
There were two of them.
There were two of them. It seems strange that the Minister of Railways found it necessary to make another examination.	.

If my hon. friend had the responsibility he would not accept the report of any other officials except those immediately responsible to him no matter how eminent they might be. Before I would take any step towards serious consideration I would want a report of a man responsible to me as I . am responsible to this House.

Surely the minister would have sufficient confidence in the men who ran the government of New Brunswick before March the 3rd to believe they would only appoint men who - were competent, straightforward, honest and trustworthy ? When the minster says he is going to make a further examination he is simply jollying the hon. member for Westmoreland.
There is a province of Quebec and a province of Nova Scotia as well as a province of New Brunswick.

Then let us know what the policy is in regard to the branch lines in New Brunswick ? The majority of this House have been cheerfully voting large sums of money for railways in all parts of the country, and it seems to me it would be far more important to take over the tributary lines of the government railways. We have granted a large subsidy for a line to Hudson bay although we know nothing of the territory through which it shall pass, and we have conflicting testimony as to the practicability of the water route when the railway is built. The minister can quite understand that one management instead of several ; that the utilization on the branch lines of the lighter rails taken from the main line, instead of selling them to favoured friendis as old junk, with tremendous profit to the men who buy and great loss to the railway which sells ; the minister knows that this would tend to great economy in the management.
The old rails on the Intercolonial have not been sold as old junk to friends of the government. They have always been put up to tender and the highest bidder got them.

Perhaps a better price may have been obtained than the hon. gen-

tleman would get for the broken pots and pans in his own house, but all the same these rails were sold as junk to be broken up. Mr. Mathew Lodge made extensive purchases of these rails and I understood he was quite a friend of the government because the government was quite a friend to him.
I dont think Mr. Lodge ever bought any rails.
Perhaps -not when my bon. friend was minister, but it was commonly. reported that he did.
I think not, but what is the point if he bought them by tender ?
1 said that these rails were sold to Mr. Lodge whom I took to be a friend of the government.
Sold by tender.

So were the timber limits and the coal lands sold by tender, but we know what happened. In certain districts in New Brunswick very great sacrifices have been made by ithe people to get these lines of railway. In one of the counties I have the honour to represent a heavy and a grievous tax was placed on the people for the purpose of getting these branch lines built. New Brunswick, compared with some other provinces, is poor in resources, but here in the great provinces of Ontario and Quebec, between Ottawa and Montreal, where there are at present three lines of railway, a fourth is being built, and it is being largely subsidized by this government; subsidized to an extent that would go a long way towards purchasing these branch lines in New Brunswick and making them part of the Intercolonial. The principle of acquiring these branch lines was adopted three or four years ago, when the government purchased the Canada Eastern. Why did they do that?
Because it was connecting with the Canadian Pacific Railway, another great trunk line.

But the Canadian Pacific already had a connection with the Intercolonial at St. John. The reason why they acquired the Canada Eastern was because of the political exigency that existed at the time, and because it was necessary to carry out a pledge whereby they had been enabled -to elect a supporter in the county of York, N.B. That is the reason why ; and at the very time that scheme went through I brought up the question of the acquisition by the government of the rest of the branch lines in the province of New Brunswick. I asked if that policy was to be adopted, and I got a very unsatisfactory reply from the then Minister of Railways. But it seems to me that if we have all the money required for these Mr. FOWLER.
various railway schemes-although the Finance Minister may have some difficulty when he comes to borrow-and if we have cheerfully voted for the building of canals in these upper provinces, which yield no revenue whatever to this Dominion, we ought to have some consideration for the maritime provinces in this regard. Take the scheme of the 'Georgian bay canal, which will cost, at the lowest estimate, about a hundred millions or, if we may judge from our experience with the Grand Trunk Pacific, will cost more than double that estimate, which would be $200,000,000, a very small portion of this would enable us to purchase all these branch lines in the province of New Brunswick. For these reasons, I do think that the government should announce its policy now in favour of the acquisition of all the branch lines which are feeders to the Intercolonial Railway. It should not be a question whether or not these branch lines are particularly profitable, but only whether the price at which they can be obtained is a fair price or not.

My hon. friend, in referring to purchase of the Canada Eastern Railway by the government, knows that he was not accurate in his statement of the object. The object of securing that line was to protect the Intercolonal in its sphere of influence, and to prevent the Canadian Pacific Railway acquiring the line and invading the territory controlled by the Intercolonial. The purchase was made at less than $6,000 per mile. It was the cheapest railway that was ever purchased in Canada; but it was for that particular purpose and for no other that the railway was acquired, as my hon. friend knows.

I find no fault with the price paid for the Canada Eastern Railway; but I do say that the purchase was not for the reason stated by the hon. member for Westmoreland, but that there was an understanding between a certain gentleman who was very prominent at that time and very influential in the county of York whereby the government party were enabled in the election of 1900 to carry the county of York for the government. The government did not carry out the terms, and session after session passed by until the election of 1904 came on, when the government found it necessary to carry out the terms, otherwise there would have been trouble. Any gentleman who was a member of this House at that time, and was acquainted with the then member for York, would know that he was calculating on this arrangement, and that he could be heard in these corridors declaiming against the government for their failure to carry it out. It was common knowledge that in the last session he was kicking all the time because that arrangement was not carried out, and finally it was I carried out. But gratitude is a lively sense

of favours yet to come, and as the railway had been bought, the people returned to their previous allegiance, and elected my hon. friend who now represents the county of York, and who will be elected again to represent it at the next election.

I had a great deal to do in the provincial legislature with urging from time to time the adoption of resolutions in favour of the acquisition of these branch roads. The hon. gentleman truly says that the government of which I was a member appointed a commission for the purpose of making an inquiry into all the branches in the province which were feeders of the Intercolonial Railway, with a view of furnishing the Minister of Railways with sucli information as would be of value in order to enable him to determine whether or not it would be desirable to take over these roads. My hon. friend has given us a bit of ancient history. What is more important to us to-day, in regard to the Canada Eastern Railway, is to know whether the acquisition of that railway was in the public interest. I say unhesitatingly that it was. The Canada Eastern has proved to be a valuable feeder of the Intercolonial, and I personally have felt, and I have not changed my view in that respect, that it would be in the interest of the public and to the advantage of the Intercolonial Railway to have it considered by an expert whether all the branches in New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Quebec would be likely to prove valuable feeders to the Intercolonial if taken over. I think my hon. friend is unfair to the Minister of Railways in suggesting that he is trying to jolly my hon. friend who represents the county of Westmoreland, who has taken a warm and earnest interest in this question. I think the Minister of Railways is pursuing a prudent course, which will commend itself to the best judgment of the people of the country when he proposes, through the officials of his department, to conduct a minute inquiry into all these branch lines in the provinces of New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Quebec. I feel sure that my hon. friend the Minister of Railways is thoroughly sincere in this. I feel that he desires to obtain the fullest possible information, and I can say for one that I am satisfied that the information which he will obtain will convince him that it will be not only in the interest of the maritime provinces, in the interest of the province of Quebec and in the interest of the whole country, but also in the interest of the Intercolonial Railway itself, that he should adopt the policy which has been adopted universally by all the great trunk lines in the country, that is, to acquire all these branches, or such of them as can be acquired on reasonable terms, which will prove valuable feeders to the Intercolonial Railway and increase its (traffic and its earning power.
428	*

It must be grateful to the Minister of Railways to get a certificate of sincerity from so sincere a person as the Minister of Public Works. The minister tells us that as a member of the local government of New Brunswick he appointed a commission to inquire and obtain for the Minister of Railways so much valuable information. It is unfortunate that he did not discuss the matter with the Minister of Railways.
That does not happen to be what I said.

I do not remember the exact words, but that is practically what he said. It is unfortunate that he did not discuss the matter with the Minister of Railways so as to learn from him whether he would consider as valuable the information which that commission was supposed to obtain. Now', the hon. Minister of Public Works is in a position, as a member of the government, to make his influence felt in regard to this matter of branch lines ; and when all these subsidies were being considered by the government, why did he not put in a word for the branch lines in New Brunswick, Nova Scotia and Quebec ?
How do you know that I did not ?

I am sure that he did not, because knowing the great influence which the hon. gentleman would have bn his colleagues, knowing the great assistance he ha* been to the government and the tremendous strength he has brought to it, which the First Minister must realize, his influence would be so great that he would be able to impose his views upon his colleagues and if he had advocated with his heart and soul and strength the construction of these branch lines they would have adopted that policy.

I think it strange when we hear so much from ministers and members on the other side about the acquisition of feeders for the Intercolonial Railway that they have said nothing about the Prince Edward Island Railway, which would be the most valuable feeder they could have for the Intercolonial Railway if a connecting link between the Intercolonial Railway and it were constructed. It seems there is either a concerted plan on the part of the government to overlook Prince Edward Island or else there is some ulterior motive in relation to the buying of these branch lines. We have had many promises of investigation and report. It seems strange that they should overlook the most profitable feeder the Intercolonial Railway could have.

Bill (No. 217) respecting the Quebec Bridge and Railway Company-Mr. Graham-read the second time and House went into committee thereon.
Has the government come to a conclusion as to whether the present site and the works there will be utilized or will some other site be chosen? Have any inquiries been made on the subject ?

The position of the government is this. Leaving aside everything that has happened, this fact stares us in the face, the Quebec bridge is down and the Quebec bridge has to go up. It is the duty of the government to see that the plan is carried out as parliament has directed. This Bill provides for taking over the enterprise in accordance with the agreement. Different opinions are expressed as to using the present site. Some members say that the present material will do. I am not offering any opinion, but I say the first duty of the government is to select a board of engineers composed of two or three of the most prominent engineers in the world. To them will be entrusted the duty of seeing if any or all of the piers, if any or all of the material or design, is adequate for the construction of the bridge. To them will be entrusted the task of selecting a design for the construction of the Quebec bridge. My idea is to submit to them the question of site as well, and to take their advice largely as to the best place to build the bridge and the design to be followed. For, whatever has happened, it must be obvious to every person that no mistakes ought to be made in the future, but that the structure to be erected there should be a lasting one and a credit to Canada, because it will be the greatest of its kind in the world.

I' hope that estimates will be made not only for the present site but also for construction by way of the Island of Orleans. It may be remembered that the objection to the Island of Orleans scheme was that it might cost $1,500,000 or $2,000,000 more. But the cost of railway terminals is also to be considered. Estimates should be made so as to show the cost of both bridge and terminals by either route. It may be that the bridge by the Island of Orleans scheme will cost more, this will be more than made up in the saving on the terminals.
Is the government to pay the bridge company anything for compensation ?
That is provided for in the agreement-the par value of the stoek with 5 per cent simple interest and the bonus of 10 per cent.
What is the amount of the stock ?
It will be $400,000.

Hon. gentlemen are inclined to guess at that. I have here the figures given me by the accountant :

Yes, if we could have sold them, but unfortunately the market is confined to only those piers needed for the bridge. Those that are there could not be built for less than $2,000,000.
I suppose the material spoken of there is under water.

No ; a great deal of it is stored. Some of the engineers claim that a great deal of it could be used. I suppose much would depend on the design of the bridge. I do no.t care to express an opinion, but it seems to me that the present site and piers will do. If the site is retained, the piers ought to be usable.
It strikes me that this is a pretty fair bargain for the company, but a pretty bad one for the country.

speechtext: Before that motion is put, while I do not object to the subject matter of the Bill, I desire to protest against this Bill taking precedence of my Bill on a very much more important subject. This House unanimously passed my Bill to amend the Railway Act early in the session, and sent it to the Senate before Christmas. It was a Bill to protect the lives of every man,'woman and child from the fatal accidents that are taking place every day at railway crossings. The Senate amended that Bill three or four months afterwards, and sent it back to this House. A week or ten days ago I asked the House to consider this Bill, and was told by the Minister of Railways that it was too late in the session, and that they could not take up any Public Bills and Orders. I think if any Bill is to be taken up, it should* bd that one.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: BUSINESS OF THE HOUSE-PUBLIC BILLS AND ORDERS.
speechtext: I would not care to offer any opinion on that point to-night. I realize now that this Bill to amend the Canada Temperance Act can not go through, unless it meets with general approval. I judge from what my hon. friend says that this Bill may be a matter of debate, I offer no opinion concerning it. But if there is no objection to this Bill, we can deal with it.
